title: The Day Creators Got Paid
hook: YouTube offered its most popular uploaders a share of the advertising. Making videos became a job.
situation: By 2007 YouTube had enormous audiences and almost no way for the people making videos to earn from them. Popular uploaders were being courted by television and could easily have left.
exchange: In May 2007 YouTube invited a small group of its most popular creators, including Smosh, LisaNova and lonelygirl15, into a Partner Program that placed adverts around their videos and shared the revenue with them.
brought: The first partners
Audiences big enough to sell to advertisers, and a reason to keep uploading.
YouTube
Advertising sales and a payment system that reached individuals, not only companies.
turning_point: The programme widened through 2007 and later opened to almost anyone who met its thresholds. Sharing advertising with ordinary uploaders became the founding business model of the creator economy.
metric_label: When YouTube first shared advertising revenue with creators
measure: A launch date. YouTube did not publish what the first partners earned
evidence: YouTube’s own announcement and contemporary reporting confirm the launch and the first partners. The scale of payments became visible only much later, and is covered in the last case of this edition.
lesson: Platforms keep their best people by sharing the money. A creator programme that pays reliably beats one that only promises exposure.
take: Every creator business in this archive rests on this decision. YouTube chose to treat uploaders as partners rather than free labour, and its competitors spent the next fifteen years catching up.
how_to_measure: For any creator revenue programme, publish the share of eligible creators who earn something each month, and the median, not only the total paid.

image.credit: Official platform graphic, substituted still; no original 2007 video authenticated · YouTube

title: Theatre Is Evil
hook: A musician left her label and asked her fans for $100,000. They gave her twelve times that.
situation: Musicians relied on record labels to fund albums and tours. Amanda Palmer had left hers after disagreements over how her work was sold, and had a dedicated fanbase she spoke to directly online.
exchange: Palmer asked fans on Kickstarter to fund an album, book and tour, offering tiers from a digital download to house concerts and art.
brought: Amanda Palmer
Years of direct contact with fans, and rewards that offered access as well as music.
Her fans
Pledges from almost 25,000 people who wanted to fund the work themselves.
turning_point: The campaign closed in June 2012 with $1,192,793, against a goal of $100,000, the most for a music project on Kickstarter at the time. It became the template for fan-funded music.
measure: Money pledged, recorded by Kickstarter and Guinness World Records. Pledges, not profit
evidence: The total is recorded by Guinness World Records. Palmer later published how much of it went on making and shipping rewards, which showed how little was left as profit, an important lesson in itself.
lesson: Fans will fund work they feel part of. Price the rewards so that delivering them doesn’t consume the money raised.
take: Palmer showed that a direct relationship with fans is a balance sheet. She also faced criticism for asking volunteer musicians to play for free, a reminder that fan funding raises expectations of fairness.

how_to_measure: Report what a campaign nets after rewards, fees and shipping, and how many backers return for the next one.

title: A Musician Builds Patreon
hook: His videos had millions of views and paid him a few hundred dollars. So he built a way for fans to pay monthly.
situation: Advertising revenue rewarded huge view counts. Creators with smaller, devoted audiences, or work that took months to make, could not live on it.
exchange: Jack Conte, one half of the band Pomplamoose, spent months on an elaborate music video and earned very little from advertising. With his college roommate Sam Yam, he founded Patreon, where fans pledge a regular amount to support a creator.
brought: Jack Conte
First-hand knowledge of the gap between views and income, and credibility with other creators.
Patrons
Small monthly payments that added up to a living for creators they cared about.
turning_point: Patreon launched in 2013. By 2025 it had passed $10 billion paid to creators by their fans, with more than $2 billion a year flowing through it.
metric_label: Paid to creators by fans on Patreon, as of 2025
measure: Total fan payments stated by Patreon and reported by Axios. Before fees and costs
evidence: The cumulative total is the company’s own figure, reported by Axios. It is a strong revenue signal because it is money paid directly by fans, although the distribution between creators is very uneven.
lesson: A smaller audience that pays every month can be worth more than a huge one that only watches. Design creator programmes for depth as well as reach.
take: Patreon is the creator economy’s most important idea after advertising sharing: that fans want to pay. It was built by a creator who had felt the problem, which is why creators trusted it.

creative.label: Watch Pedals and the original Patreon pitch · Jack Conte
creative.heading: Creator media

impact_source: Read about the $10 billion milestone · Axios
how_to_measure: For membership programmes, track monthly retention of paying members and revenue per creator by size band, so the middle of the market is visible as well as the top.

title: Disney Buys a YouTube Network
hook: A network of YouTubers founded by creators sold to Disney for at least $500 million. Within three years most of them were gone.
situation: Multi-channel networks bundled thousands of YouTube channels, sold advertising across them and took a share of creators’ income. Media companies wanted young audiences and saw networks as a shortcut.
exchange: Maker Studios, founded by YouTubers including Lisa Donovan, Ben Donovan, Danny Zappin and Shay Carl, grew into one of the largest networks. Disney agreed to buy it for $500 million, with up to $450 million more if targets were met.
brought: Maker Studios
Tens of thousands of channels and a pipeline of young talent.
Disney
Capital, characters and a plan to bring its brands to YouTube audiences.
turning_point: The deal in March 2014 made creator networks look like the future of media. By 2017 Disney had cut Maker from tens of thousands of channels to around 300 and folded it into a new division.
metric_label: Upfront price, with up to $950 million in total
measure: The announced price. Disney did not report what Maker earned after the purchase
evidence: The price and later restructuring are well documented. They show the value placed on creator audiences and how hard it was for a traditional owner to keep that value.
deal_value: $500 million upfront, up to $950 million with performance payments
lesson: Buying access to creators is not the same as owning their audiences. Creators stay where they are respected and paid fairly.
take: Maker is the moment old media tried to buy the creator economy whole. What it learned is that a network is only as strong as the creators’ willingness to stay in it.
announcement: Read about the deal · CNN Money
impact_source: Read about the deal terms · Tubefilter
how_to_measure: After buying a creator business, track creator retention, revenue per channel and audience overlap with the parent’s own brands every quarter.

image.alt: The Disney wordmark above the Maker Studios name in black and white

title: Amazon Buys Twitch
hook: People watching other people play games looked like a niche. Amazon paid almost a billion dollars in cash for it.
situation: Twitch grew out of Justin.tv, a site built around one founder streaming his life. Its gaming section took off as players broadcast their games and audiences gathered to chat and subscribe.
exchange: Streamers built communities that watched for hours at a time, paying for subscriptions and emotes. Twitch, run by Emmett Shear and Justin Kan’s team, became the home of live gaming.
brought: Twitch’s streamers
Hours of live entertainment every day and fiercely loyal chat communities.
Amazon
Cash, infrastructure and a long-term bet on live video.
turning_point: In August 2014 Amazon bought Twitch for $970 million in cash, after reports that Google had been close to a deal. Live streaming was confirmed as a format worth owning.
metric_label: Price Amazon paid in cash, August 2014
measure: The purchase price, confirmed by Twitch
evidence: The deal is documented. It values the platform the streamers built rather than paying the streamers themselves, which is part of the lesson.
lesson: Long, live viewing sessions are valuable to whoever owns the relationship. Creators should know who owns the platform before building their business on it.
take: Amazon paid for a habit that streamers had created. Ten years on, the fights over revenue splits and exclusive deals all trace back to that imbalance.

title: Exploding Kittens
hook: A webcomic artist and two game designers asked for $10,000 for a card game. More than 219,000 people backed it.
situation: Board and card games reached shops through publishers. Crowdfunding was growing, but most campaigns aimed for tens of thousands of dollars.
exchange: Matthew Inman, creator of the webcomic The Oatmeal, made a card game with designers Elan Lee and Shane Small and launched it on Kickstarter with his drawings and humour.
brought: Matthew Inman
A huge readership and an art style instantly recognisable to them.
Elan Lee and Shane Small
Game design that made a simple idea playable.
turning_point: The campaign ended in February 2015 with $8,782,571 from 219,382 backers, the most backers of any Kickstarter project at that point. Exploding Kittens became a games company with retail distribution and a Netflix series.
metric_label: Backers, the most of any Kickstarter project at the time
measure: Backer count and money pledged, recorded by Kickstarter
evidence: Kickstarter’s figures are public and were widely reported. They are paid pledges, a strong signal of demand. Later sales built on the campaign but are not part of this figure.
lesson: A creator’s audience can launch a product category the creator has never worked in. Partner with specialists to make the product good.
take: The Oatmeal turned readers into customers for a game, not a comic. It shows that what an audience trusts is the creator’s taste, which travels further than the original medium.
credit: Matthew Inman, Elan Lee and Shane Small, 2015

creative.label: Watch the original Kickstarter campaign · Matthew Inman
creative.heading: Creator media

impact_source: Read the final figures · Crowdfund Insider
how_to_measure: Track backers who were already readers, then follow retail sales in the year after delivery to see if the product found buyers beyond the creator’s audience.

title: The First Rich List
hook: Forbes added up what YouTubers earned for the first time. A Swedish gamer topped it at $12 million.
situation: By 2015 YouTube stars were famous, but their income was a mystery. Parents, advertisers and the press assumed they earned little beyond pocket money.
exchange: Forbes estimated the pre-tax earnings of YouTube’s biggest stars from advertising, sponsorships, merchandise and other deals, and published its first ranking.
brought: The creators
Businesses big enough to estimate, from advertising to books and tours.
Forbes
A familiar rich-list format that made creator income headline news.
turning_point: PewDiePie came first with an estimated $12 million, ahead of Smosh, Fine Bros and Lindsey Stirling. The annual list made creator earnings a story the mainstream press followed every year.
metric_label: PewDiePie’s estimated earnings, the top of the first list
measure: A Forbes estimate of pre-tax earnings, not a disclosed figure
evidence: The list is a published estimate from interviews and industry data. It shows the scale people believed creators had reached, not audited income.
lesson: Creator income is diversified from early on. Brands negotiating with top creators are dealing with businesses, not hobbyists.
take: The rich list did for creators what box-office charts did for films: it gave everyone a number to argue about. It also helped persuade a generation that making videos was a career.

creative.label: Read about the list · The Drum
creative.heading: Creator media

announcement: Read about the list · The Drum
how_to_measure: When estimating a creator’s commercial value, separate platform income from deals and products. The mix tells you how dependent they are on one platform.

image.credit: Creator commentary on earnings, July 2015; predates the October Forbes ranking · PewDiePie

title: Super Chat
hook: Viewers could pay to make their comment stand out. Live chat became a till.
situation: Twitch streamers earned from tips and subscriptions while they broadcast. YouTube’s live streamers had only advertising and a little-used fan-funding button.
exchange: In January 2017 YouTube launched Super Chat, letting viewers pay to highlight and pin their message in a live stream’s chat, with the money shared with the creator. It replaced the old fan-funding feature.
brought: Live streamers
Shows where reading and reacting to chat was part of the entertainment.
YouTube
Payments built into the chat, available in many countries at once.
turning_point: Super Chat made paying a creator a public, social act. It became a core income for live streamers on YouTube and, later, for virtual YouTubers, whose fans gave some of the largest totals on the platform.
measure: A launch date. YouTube has not published Super Chat totals
evidence: The launch is documented by YouTube and the trade press. Ranking sites later tracked Super Chat totals per channel, but YouTube has not confirmed them.
lesson: Paying is more attractive when others can see it. Give fans a way to support creators that also earns them recognition in the community.
take: Super Chat turned tipping into a performance. The creators who did best treated every paid message as a moment in the show, not a transaction.
impact_source: Read how it replaced fan funding · Tubefilter
how_to_measure: Track paid messages per thousand live viewers and the share of payers who pay again within a month.

image.alt: A phone interface showing a creator livestream above viewer chat messages
image.credit: Official 2017 Super Chat launch demonstration graphic · YouTube

title: The First Paid Substack
hook: An expert on China charged readers for his newsletter. A new platform was built around him.
situation: Writers depended on publications for income. Independent newsletters existed, but charging for one meant stitching together payment tools and email software.
exchange: Bill Bishop, who had written Sinocism, a newsletter on China, for years, became the first writer to launch a paid publication on Substack, a new service built to make subscription newsletters simple.
brought: Bill Bishop
Deep expertise and readers who relied on his daily analysis.
Substack
Payments and publishing in one place, taking a share of subscription revenue.
turning_point: Substack launched publicly with Sinocism in October 2017. Within a few years it had thousands of paid newsletters, and writers left newsrooms to build their own subscription businesses.
metric_label: When Sinocism launched as Substack’s first paid newsletter
measure: A launch date. Bishop’s revenue has not been disclosed in full
evidence: The launch is documented by TechCrunch and Substack. Bishop has described his business in interviews, but subscriber and revenue figures are not public.
lesson: Specialist knowledge commands a subscription. A small audience that needs what you know can support a business.
take: Sinocism proves the creator economy is not only video. A writer with expertise and a mailing list owns his audience in a way no YouTuber ever fully can.

creative.label: Read Five Years of Substack, with Bill Bishop
creative.heading: Creator media

how_to_measure: For a paid newsletter, track the conversion rate from free to paid readers, annual renewal and revenue per thousand subscribers.

title: The Legend of Vox Machina
hook: Voice actors played Dungeons & Dragons on a live stream. Fans paid $11 million for a cartoon of it.
situation: Animated series were funded by studios and networks. A web show about a tabletop game had a devoted following but no obvious route to television.
exchange: The cast of Critical Role, who streamed their campaign weekly, asked fans on Kickstarter to fund a 22-minute animated special based on their first story.
brought: Critical Role
Years of weekly streams and a community that knew every character.
The Critters
88,887 backers who funded the project in hours, then funded much more.
turning_point: The $750,000 goal was hit in under an hour. The campaign closed in April 2019 with $11,385,449, the most-funded film or television project on Kickstarter. Amazon then commissioned two seasons.
metric_label: Raised for an animated series on Kickstarter
measure: Money pledged, recorded by Kickstarter and reported by CNBC
evidence: Kickstarter’s figures are public. The later Amazon order shows the campaign worked as proof of demand for a studio.
lesson: A crowdfunding total can be the pitch to a studio. Fans who pay up front are evidence a commissioner can’t ignore.
take: Critical Role used crowdfunding as market research and won a series deal with the result. It is the cleanest example in the archive of a community proving demand before a company would.

creative.label: Watch the original Kickstarter launch · Critical Role
creative.heading: Creator media

announcement: Read how the campaign closed · CNBC
impact_source: Read about the Amazon order · Tubefilter
how_to_measure: Use a pre-sale as a test: measure backers per thousand engaged viewers, and the share from outside the core community.

image.credit: Original 2019 Kickstarter campaign launch · Critical Role

title: The $200 Million Creator Fund
hook: TikTok promised its creators $200 million. Many found the payments worth a few cents a thousand views.
situation: TikTok’s creators drove its growth but had little way to earn on the platform itself. Rivals were courting its stars, and the app faced political pressure in the United States.
exchange: In July 2020 TikTok launched a $200 million fund for US creators, saying it would grow to $1 billion over three years, paid according to views and engagement.
brought: TikTok’s creators
The videos that kept hundreds of millions of people scrolling.
TikTok
A fixed pot of money divided among eligible creators.
turning_point: Because the pot was fixed while the number of creators grew, many reported falling pay per view. TikTok replaced the fund in 2023 with a programme paying more for longer videos.
measure: A commitment, not a record of payments. Individual payouts were reported by creators, not by TikTok
evidence: The fund’s size is from TikTok’s own announcement. Creators’ complaints about low payouts were widely reported, and TikTok’s decision to replace it confirms the model had problems.
deal_value: $200 million, rising to a promised $1 billion over three years
lesson: A fixed fund shared among a growing number of creators pays each of them less over time. Revenue sharing scales; a pot doesn’t.
take: The Creator Fund was a headline, not a business model. It is a useful warning for any brand or platform designing creator incentives: people work out quickly what they are worth.
impact_source: Read about the $1 billion plan · Tubefilter
how_to_measure: Publish payments per thousand views by month. If the rate falls as more creators join, the model needs to change before the best creators leave.

image.alt: TikTok Creator Fund lettering on a dark background
image.credit: Official 2020 Creator Fund announcement graphic, cropped to the title · TikTok

title: Call Her Daddy
hook: She left the company that owned her show and kept the name. Then she signed two of the biggest deals in podcasting.
situation: Call Her Daddy began in 2018 under Barstool Sports, which owned the show. When the host wanted better terms, the question of who owned a podcast’s name and audience became public.
exchange: Alex Cooper won control of the show in 2021 and licensed it exclusively to Spotify in a deal reported at $60 million. In 2024 she moved to SiriusXM for a reported $125 million, keeping the rights to her show.
brought: Alex Cooper
A huge young audience, a distinct voice and the show’s name.
Spotify and SiriusXM
Guaranteed money and distribution in exchange for exclusive rights.
turning_point: The deals made Cooper one of the highest-paid podcasters and showed that the host, not the original publisher, held the value of a creator-led show.
metric_label: Reported value of the SiriusXM deal, 2024
measure: A reported deal value, including performance elements. Not disclosed in full by either side
evidence: Both deals were widely reported by The Wrap, CNN and others. The terms were not published in full, so the figures are reported rather than confirmed.
deal_value: $60 million with Spotify (2021, reported) and $125 million with SiriusXM (2024, reported)
lesson: Own the name and the audience relationship. A creator who controls the rights can license them, again and again.
take: Cooper’s story is about ownership more than money. She fought to keep the name, and every later deal was possible because she did.

impact_source: Read about the move from Spotify · CNN
how_to_measure: For a licensing deal, track audience retention after the move, advertising revenue per listener and growth from the new partner’s distribution.

title: Shorts Get a Share
hook: YouTube decided short videos would earn a share of advertising, not a bonus from a fund.
situation: YouTube launched Shorts to compete with TikTok and paid creators through a $100 million fund. Like TikTok’s fund, it was a fixed pot and creators wanted something that grew with the platform.
exchange: From 1 February 2023 YouTube pooled advertising revenue from Shorts and gave 45% of the creators’ portion to them, through the Partner Program, with new thresholds for eligibility.
brought: Shorts creators
Billions of daily views on short vertical videos.
YouTube
An advertising system that already paid long-form creators, extended to a new format.
turning_point: Shorts moved from a fund to revenue sharing, setting a model that rivals had to answer. It tied creators’ income to the platform’s advertising growth.
metric_label: Share of the Shorts creator pool paid to creators
measure: The revenue share announced by YouTube. Actual payments per view vary and are not published
evidence: The model is documented by YouTube and the trade press. How much it pays per thousand views varies widely, and YouTube has not published averages.
lesson: Revenue sharing tells creators they are partners in a platform’s growth. A fund tells them they are a cost.
take: This is the Partner Program decision made again, sixteen years later, for a new format. It shows YouTube’s view that sharing advertising is what keeps creators.

creative.medium: Official January 2023 Partner Program contract explanation
creative.label: Watch the January 2023 contract explanation · YouTube Creators
creative.heading: Creator media

impact_source: Read about the start date · Android Central
how_to_measure: Compare revenue per thousand views for short and long videos by the same creator, and track whether Shorts viewers go on to watch long-form.

image.credit: Official January 2023 Partner Program contract explanation · YouTube Creators

title: The $100 Million Stream
hook: A new platform paid one streamer more than many sports stars earn. The price of a creator’s audience had changed.
situation: Twitch dominated live streaming and its biggest streamers had few alternatives. New rivals needed audiences fast, and the quickest way was to pay for the streamers who brought them.
exchange: Félix Lengyel, known as xQc and one of Twitch’s most-watched streamers, signed a two-year, non-exclusive deal with Kick reported at $70 million, rising to $100 million with incentives.
brought: xQc
Very long daily streams and one of the largest live audiences in the world.
Kick
Guaranteed payment, a creator-friendly revenue split and freedom to stream elsewhere.
turning_point: The deal in June 2023 was recognised by Guinness World Records as the largest streaming deal for an individual. It forced other platforms to rethink how they paid and kept their streamers.
metric_label: Reported maximum value of the Kick deal
measure: A reported deal value, $70 million base plus incentives. Not published by Kick in full
evidence: The deal was widely reported and recorded by Guinness World Records. Kick’s ownership links to a gambling company drew criticism, which is part of the context.
deal_value: $70 million base, up to $100 million, reported
lesson: When platforms compete for creators, the creators set the price. Keep relationships close before a rival makes an offer.
take: This deal is the creator economy’s transfer fee. It also shows the questions to ask about where the money comes from before you follow it.

title: Seventy Billion Dollars
hook: Seventeen years after the Partner Program, YouTube said it had paid out more than $70 billion in three years.
situation: Creator income had grown into an economy, but platforms rarely disclosed what they paid. Creators, regulators and investors had to rely on estimates.
exchange: In his February 2024 letter, YouTube’s chief executive Neal Mohan said the platform had paid more than $70 billion to creators, artists and media companies over the previous three years.
brought: YouTube’s creators
The videos, music and shows that generated the advertising and subscription revenue.
YouTube
Advertising, YouTube Premium and the payment system built on the 2007 Partner Program.
turning_point: The figure put a scale on the business model that started in 2007. It also fed debate over how the money was shared between the largest media companies and individual creators.
metric_label: Paid to creators, artists and media companies, 2021 to 2023
measure: A total disclosed by YouTube. It includes music labels and media companies, not only independent creators
evidence: The figure comes from YouTube’s chief executive and was widely reported. It is an actual payment total, but YouTube does not break it down by type of partner.
lesson: Revenue sharing at scale builds an industry. The breakdown, who gets what, matters as much as the total.
take: This closes the loop on the edition’s first case. The Partner Program became the largest creator payment system in the world, and the next argument is about how fairly it shares.

how_to_measure: Ask platforms to report payouts by partner type and size band: individual creators, music and media companies, and the share reaching the smallest earners.
